title: Everyday Customs in Japan and France
summary: First, we look at Japanese greetings and how bowing and greeting words change with time and status. Next, we enter a Japanese home and follow the shoes-and-slippers steps.

cover.alt: A guest in an amber sweater and a host in a green cardigan bow at a Japanese home entrance. Outdoor shoes sit below the wooden step, with indoor slippers above it.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: First, we look at Japanese greetings and how bowing and greeting words change with time and status. Next, we enter a Japanese home and follow the shoes-and-slippers steps. Then we sit at the table in Japan and at a restaurant in France. Finally, we see why Japan has no tipping custom and how its fast trains stay on time.

items.prompt: How do you greet a friend, and how do you greet your boss? Is there a difference?
Do you take off your shoes when you go into your home or a friend's home?
When you eat in a restaurant, do you leave extra money for the staff? Why or why not?

blocks.title: Part 1: A Greeting That Carries Information
paragraphs: Imagine two people meet at a Japanese office in the morning. Later, they meet again in the evening. They do not just say the same "hello" both times. A Japanese greeting changes with the time of day and with the people.

In Japan, bowing is the common greeting. But not every bow is the same. The bow changes with social status, so it depends on who is greeting whom. A bow to a senior manager is not the same as a bow to a friend. The words change too. People say "konnichiwa" in the daytime and "konbanwa" in the evening. They use these words when they meet someone for the first time that day.

So a Japanese greeting does more than say "I see you." It also shows the time of day and how the two people are connected. You can think of it like the address on a letter. It is short, but it tells you where the letter is going. In the same way, a short bow tells both people something about their relationship.
For a visitor, this has a practical side. You do not need a perfect bow. But it helps to notice that greetings in Japan follow the situation. They are not one fixed action.

images.alt: Two office greetings: a woman in green bows more deeply than an older man in blue, while she and a woman in amber exchange similar bows in the neighboring scene.

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: A Greeting That Carries Information

items.prompt: What two things can change a Japanese greeting?
items.answer: The time of day changes the words, with "konnichiwa" in the daytime and "konbanwa" in the evening. Social status changes the bow.
items.explanation:
In your language, do greetings change with the time of day or with the other person's status? Give an example.

Think about how people greet each other in France or the USA. How might a Japanese visitor feel about those greetings, and why?

blocks.title: Part 2: A Home With Clear Borders
paragraphs: Now imagine a Japanese colleague invites you to their home. This is a bigger moment than it may seem. Being invited to a Japanese home is an honour. Many Japanese people feel their homes are humble, which means simple or not special enough for guests. So when someone opens their home to you, they are giving you something important.

Inside the home, you will find clear borders, and each border has its own rule. At the entrance, people take off their shoes. Then they put on indoor slippers. When they step onto tatami, the straw mats on some floors, they take off the slippers too. The bathroom is another border. People take off their slippers there, and sometimes they put on special bathroom slippers instead.

So one short walk through a house can mean more than one change of footwear. The rule is not just "no shoes inside." The rule is that different parts of the home have different steps. The entrance, the main rooms, the tatami room and the bathroom each have their own.

Think of it like the doors at an airport. You pass one gate and follow one rule. Then you pass the next gate and follow another. A guest who follows these steps shows that they understand the home and respect the invitation.

blocks.title: Check: Part 2: A Home With Clear Borders

items.prompt: After you take off your shoes at the entrance, what are the next footwear steps in a Japanese home?
items.answer: You put on indoor slippers. You take off the slippers on tatami mats or in the bathroom. In the bathroom, you sometimes change into special bathroom slippers.
items.explanation: Why do you think the borders inside a Japanese home are so clear? What could they show about how people think of different spaces?

blocks.title: Part 3: Rules That Protect the Table
paragraphs: At a Japanese meal, the table is a shared space. Many rules exist to keep that space fair for everyone. Before eating, people say "itadakimasu," a word of thanks at the start of the meal. They also wait until everyone is ready before they start eating. Nobody runs ahead of the group.

Shared dishes are common. Everyone takes food from the same plates, so small actions matter. If one piece of food is left, it is polite to ask before you take the last bite. Leaving food on your own plate is seen as rude. Together, these rules work like the rules of a team game. Each person plays their part, so the whole table has a good meal.

Some rules are more flexible than visitors expect. Sushi, for example, can be eaten with chopsticks or with your hands. So the point is not to make every action strict. The point is to respect the food and the other people at the table.

France shows a different place where manners begin. In a French restaurant, the rules start at the door, before any food arrives. Staff usually give guests a table. Customers wait at the entrance until someone takes them to a table. If you want a different table, you can ask, but you should ask politely. In Japan, the clearest rules are around sharing the food. In France, an important rule comes at the start: let the staff guide you.

images.alt: At a Japanese dining table, two women wait beside a shared sushi platter as a man pulls out his chair. In a French restaurant, the women wait as a waiter gestures toward an empty table.

blocks.title: Check: Part 3: Rules That Protect the Table

items.prompt: Why is it polite to ask before taking the last bite at a Japanese meal?
items.answer: Because dishes are often shared, so the last piece belongs to the whole table, not just to you.
items.explanation: Which is harder for you: waiting at a French restaurant door for a table, or waiting for everyone before eating at a Japanese table? Why?

blocks.title: Part 4: Polite Service Without Tips
paragraphs: Here is a question many visitors ask: if you do not tip, why would the service be good? In Japan, tipping is generally not practised. Sometimes a service charge is already part of the price. But Japanese service is known for being very polite and careful. So the missing tip does not mean missing effort.

The reason lies in an idea about customers. In Japan, the customer is treated almost like a god. Good service is part of the job and part of the price, not an extra that you pay for at the end. If you leave money on the table, it can seem strange, because the work was already expected.
Paying has its own manners too. It is proper to put your money on a small tray, not to hand it straight to the person. Like the slippers at a doorway, the tray is a small step that shows care.

So the link between money and service is different here. In some places, a tip is a way to say "thank you for good service." In Japan, the thank-you is already part of the system, and the service is the starting point.

blocks.title: Check: Part 4: Polite Service Without Tips

items.prompt: Why does no tipping in Japan not mean poor service?
items.answer: Because very polite service is part of the job and the price. The customer is treated almost like a god, and sometimes a service charge is already included.
items.explanation: Would you prefer service where tips are expected or service where the tip is part of the price? Why?

blocks.title: Part 5: Small Care at a Very Large Scale
paragraphs: All these customs share one habit: careful attention to small steps. You can see the same habit in Japan's fast trains. The Tokaido Shinkansen is a high-speed line in Japan. In 2024, it ran 383 trains a day and carried about 460,000 passengers.

Those trains had an average delay of just 1.4 minutes per train. That is about 84 seconds. Now think about the size of the job. If 460,000 people share 383 trains, that is about 1,200 people per train on average. Each person must get on and off quickly, every train must leave on time, and this happens all day.

This is where the small habits matter. A delay on one train can spread to the next one, like a line of people at a shop. When one person stops, everyone behind them waits too. So a short average delay is not only about fast machines. It also depends on many small, careful actions, repeated hundreds of times a day.

Bowing to the right person, changing slippers at the right door and leaving a train exactly on time may seem very different. But they all show the same thing: people paying close attention to the small step in front of them.

images.alt: Two women wait behind the yellow tactile strip while a man carrying a briefcase steps off a white-and-blue train through a clear doorway.

blocks.title: Check: Part 5: Small Care at a Very Large Scale

items.prompt: In 2024, how many trains did the Tokaido Shinkansen run each day, and what was the average delay?
items.answer: It ran 383 trains a day, and the average delay was 1.4 minutes per train.
items.explanation: Do you think a culture of careful small steps could work on the trains in your country? What would need to change?

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: At the start, you may have thought that being "nice" works the same way everywhere. In fact, customs in Japan follow clear steps tied to time, status, space and the group, and France has its own steps, even at a restaurant door. No tipping in Japan does not mean less care, because care is already part of the job.

items.prompt: Which Japanese or French custom from this lesson would be hardest for you to follow, and why?
Choose one custom from your own country. What could it show about what people there value?
How might a visitor from France or the USA explain their greetings or tipping habits to a Japanese friend?
